title: Practice Set 5 — Adding and Transforming Columns
description: Apply column transformation techniques: type casting with silent null detection, string cleaning, date extraction, arithmetic, conditional logic with when/otherwise, boolean flags, and a complete enrichment pipeline.

datasets.description: NordGrid raw Bronze meter readings with messy string data. 100 rows. All columns are strings — daily_kw and date need casting. Region values have mixed case and whitespace.

columns.name: daily_kw
columns.description: Daily energy as a raw string — includes numbers, empty strings, and unparseable values like 'N/A' and 'ERR'

columns.name: region
columns.description: Region code with inconsistent casing ('NORTH', 'north', 'North') and whitespace ('  NORTH', 'EAST  ')

characteristics.unparseableValues: 4 rows have daily_kw values that cannot be cast to double: 'N/A', 'ERR', '--', 'null'
characteristics.negatives: 3 rows have negative daily_kw values (as strings)
characteristics.totalNullsAfterCast: 8 rows will have null daily_kw after casting (4 empty + 4 unparseable)
characteristics.messyRegions: 14 distinct raw values including 'NORTH', 'north', 'North', '  NORTH', 'NORTH  ', etc.

tasks.title: Cast NordGrid's Raw Readings to Proper Types

description.context: NordGrid's Bronze meter CSV stores every column as a string. The Silver pipeline must cast daily_kw to DoubleType and date to DateType before any calculations or date operations can work. However, some daily_kw values are not valid numbers — they contain strings like 'N/A' and 'ERR' from the source system. Spark will silently convert these to null during the cast.
description.task: Read PS5_data_readings_raw.csv (header=True, no inferSchema — let all columns remain as strings). Then: (1) count how many nulls exist in daily_kw before casting and store in null_before; (2) cast daily_kw to double using withColumn and cast(); (3) cast date to date type using withColumn and cast(); (4) count how many nulls exist in daily_kw after casting and store in null_after. Store the casted DataFrame in a variable called df_typed.
description.validationHint: Before casting, there are 4 empty-string rows that read as null. After casting, 4 additional unparseable values ('N/A', 'ERR', '--', 'null') also become null — total 8.

tasks.partialCredit: 5 independent assertions. Each passed assertion earns 1/5 credit.

fields.label: Bronze loaded as strings. After `withColumn('daily_kw', col('daily_kw').cast('double'))`, the null count jumps from 4 to 8. Why?
options: Cast silently converts unparseable strings ('N/A', 'ERR', '--', 'null') to null in addition to the 4 empty-string rows that were already null
Spark fails the cast on bad strings and replaces all 100 rows with null until the bad rows are fixed
withColumn replaces the column entirely so the original null count is reset and we now see all malformed rows
fields.correctAnswer: Cast silently converts unparseable strings ('N/A', 'ERR', '--', 'null') to null in addition to the 4 empty-string rows that were already null
fields.rationale: Cast is failure-silent: any string that can't be parsed as the target type becomes null. The 4 unparseable values join the 4 originally-null rows.

tasks.title: Standardize NordGrid's Region Codes

description.context: NordGrid's source CSV exports region codes with inconsistent formatting. The same region appears as 'NORTH', 'north', 'North', '  NORTH', and 'NORTH  ' across different batch files. Downstream joins with the substation reference table fail silently because ' NORTH' does not match 'NORTH'. The Silver pipeline must standardize all region values to uppercase with no leading or trailing whitespace.
description.task: Read PS5_data_readings_raw.csv (header=True, inferSchema=True). Apply trim() and upper() to the region column using withColumn() to standardize all values. Store the result in a variable called df_clean. Then count the distinct region values and store the count in a variable called region_count.
description.validationHint: Before cleaning, there are 14 distinct region values. After cleaning, there should be exactly 4: NORTH, SOUTH, EAST, WEST.

tasks.partialCredit: 4 independent assertions. Each passed assertion earns 1/4 credit.

fields.label: Source has 'NORTH', 'north', '  NORTH', 'NORTH  ' for the same region. Which transform yields one canonical value?
options: df.withColumn('region', upper(trim(col('region')))) — trim whitespace first, then uppercase
df.withColumn('region', upper(col('region'))) — uppercase covers casing, downstream joins normalize whitespace anyway
df.withColumn('region', col('region').rlike('^NORTH$')) — a regex match returns the canonical token
fields.correctAnswer: df.withColumn('region', upper(trim(col('region')))) — trim whitespace first, then uppercase
fields.rationale: Both trim AND upper are needed: ' NORTH' and 'NORTH' differ in whitespace, 'north' and 'NORTH' differ in case. A regex returns boolean, not a value.

description.context: when().otherwise() is Spark's IF/ELSE chain. The chain evaluates conditions TOP-TO-BOTTOM and returns the FIRST one that is TRUE. If no condition matches, otherwise() catches everything left over. Two traps to know: (1) Strict < uses STRICT less-than, so the boundary value goes to the NEXT tier — daily_kw = 500 is NOT < 500, so it falls to the second when. (2) when conditions on null values evaluate to NULL (not TRUE, not FALSE) — null fails all when checks and falls all the way through to otherwise(). Same for negative values: the chain has no explicit guard, so -50 satisfies < 500 and gets classified as 'low' just like a legitimate low-usage meter.
description.task: For each sample reading, predict the tier the chain assigns.
description.validationHint: The when() chain evaluates from top to bottom and returns the first matching condition. If no condition matches and otherwise() is present, the otherwise value is used. If daily_kw is null, all comparisons evaluate to null (not true), so no when() condition matches.

evidence.label: Tier assignment logic
evidence.content:
df = df.withColumn('tier',
    when(col('daily_kw') < 500, 'low')
    .when(col('daily_kw') < 2000, 'medium')
    .when(col('daily_kw') < 4000, 'high')
    .otherwise('critical')
)
# Sample readings:
# A: 499.9    B: 500.0    C: 2000.0    E: null    F: -50.0

fields.label: Reading A (daily_kw = 499.9): which tier?
options: low — 499.9 < 500 is TRUE, so the first when() matches and returns 'low'.
medium — 499.9 is just under 500 but rounds up at the boundary, so it lands in the medium tier.
high — values close to 500 are treated as transitional and assigned to the high tier for safety.
critical — only exact tier boundaries match cleanly; in-between values fall through to otherwise.
fields.correctAnswer: low — 499.9 < 500 is TRUE, so the first when() matches and returns 'low'.
fields.rationale: 499.9 < 500 evaluates TRUE; the first when fires and returns 'low'. The most common Junior confusion is overthinking the question — when chains are simple sequential matchers; the FIRST true condition wins.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: No rounding occurs in when(); strict < uses literal numeric comparison.

Option C: There is no 'transitional' tier rule; the chain only reads literal predicates.

Option D: otherwise only catches values that fail every when().

fields.label: Reading B (daily_kw = 500.0): which tier?
options: low — 500 is the LOW threshold so it stays in the low tier; thresholds are inclusive by default.
medium — 500 < 500 is FALSE (strict less-than), so the first when fails. 500 < 2000 is TRUE, so the second when fires and returns 'medium'.
high — boundary values are pushed up two tiers for conservative classification.
critical — values exactly at a threshold fail all when() conditions and fall to otherwise.
fields.correctAnswer: medium — 500 < 500 is FALSE (strict less-than), so the first when fails. 500 < 2000 is TRUE, so the second when fires and returns 'medium'.
fields.rationale: Strict < means the boundary value belongs to the NEXT tier. 500 is not less than 500, so the first condition is false; 500 IS less than 2000, so the second fires. The most common Junior confusion is reading < as 'less than or equal' (inclusive); use <= for inclusive lower bounds.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: < is strict; 500 is not in the < 500 bucket.

Option C: No 'push up two tiers' rule exists.

Option D: 500 < 2000 is true, so otherwise is not reached.

fields.label: Reading C (daily_kw = 2000.0): which tier?
options: low — 2000 wraps around to the low tier because 4000 is the cap and 2000 is its midpoint.
medium — 2000 < 2000 is treated as TRUE in PySpark when the operands are equal floats.
high — 2000 < 500 is FALSE. 2000 < 2000 is FALSE. 2000 < 4000 is TRUE, so the third when fires and returns 'high'.
critical — exact threshold values always fall through every when() to otherwise.
fields.correctAnswer: high — 2000 < 500 is FALSE. 2000 < 2000 is FALSE. 2000 < 4000 is TRUE, so the third when fires and returns 'high'.
fields.rationale: Same boundary rule applies again: 2000 is not < 2000, so the second when fails; it IS < 4000, so the third fires. The most common Junior confusion is consistency — students get the first boundary right (500 → medium) but apply different logic to the second (2000 → medium); the rule is identical at every threshold.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: No wrap-around logic exists in when().

Option B: < is strict; equal floats give FALSE.

Option D: 2000 < 4000 is true, so otherwise is not reached.

fields.label: Reading E (daily_kw = null): which tier?
options: low — null is treated as 0 in numeric comparisons, so null < 500 evaluates to TRUE.
medium — null comparisons default to the middle tier as a sensible safe choice.
high — Spark treats null as a maximum unknown value, satisfying < 4000 but not the smaller bounds.
critical — null < 500 evaluates to NULL (not TRUE), null < 2000 → NULL, null < 4000 → NULL; no when matches, so otherwise('critical') fires.
fields.correctAnswer: critical — null < 500 evaluates to NULL (not TRUE), null < 2000 → NULL, null < 4000 → NULL; no when matches, so otherwise('critical') fires.
fields.rationale: Three-valued logic: NULL < anything is NULL, not TRUE and not FALSE. when() only fires on TRUE, so null rows fail every when condition and fall to otherwise. The most common Junior confusion is expecting null to either crash or get a null tier label; in reality null gets whatever otherwise returns, which is the OPPOSITE of what most engineers want. Fix: add when(col('daily_kw').isNull(), 'unknown') as the FIRST when clause.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: null is not coerced to 0.

Option B: No 'default to middle tier' rule exists.

Option C: null is not 'maximum'; it has no order at all.

fields.label: Reading F (daily_kw = -50.0): which tier?
options: low — -50 < 500 is TRUE, so the first when fires and returns 'low'. Negative values are NOT special-cased — they pass the same numeric comparison as legitimate low readings.
medium — negative values are floored to 0 and reclassified as medium for safety.
high — Spark detects out-of-range values and routes them to high tier for review.
critical — negative readings fail all when conditions because of sign-mismatch and fall to otherwise.
fields.correctAnswer: low — -50 < 500 is TRUE, so the first when fires and returns 'low'. Negative values are NOT special-cased — they pass the same numeric comparison as legitimate low readings.
fields.rationale: The when chain has no guard against negatives. -50 < 500 is unambiguously TRUE, so the first when fires. The pipeline silently mixes faulty sensor readings with real low-usage meters. The most common Junior confusion is assuming Spark 'knows' negatives are bad data; in reality the engineer must add an explicit when(col('daily_kw') < 0, 'invalid') guard or filter them out before the tier step.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: No flooring is applied; -50 stays -50.

Option C: No range detection logic exists.

Option D: -50 < 500 is TRUE; otherwise is not reached.

tasks.title: Enrich NordGrid Readings with Temporal Fields

description.context: NordGrid's Silver layer requires temporal fields derived from the reading date: year, month, and quarter for partitioning and reporting. The operations team also needs a daily_mw column (daily_kw divided by 1,000) for capacity reports that use megawatts instead of kilowatts. All values should be rounded to 3 decimal places.
description.task: Read PS5_data_readings_raw.csv (header=True, inferSchema=True). Cast the date column to DateType. Then add four new columns using withColumn(): (1) year extracted from date, (2) month extracted from date, (3) quarter extracted from date, and (4) daily_mw computed as daily_kw / 1000, rounded to 3 decimal places. Store the result in a variable called df_enriched.
description.validationHint: All dates are in March 2026, so year should be 2026, month should be 3, and quarter should be 1 for every row. daily_mw should be roughly 0.080 to 4.500 for valid readings.

tasks.partialCredit: 6 independent assertions. Each passed assertion earns 1/6 credit.

fields.label: How do you derive year, month, quarter from a date column AND add daily_mw = daily_kw / 1000 rounded to 3?
options: Cast date → DateType, then chain withColumn for year(col), month(col), quarter(col), and round(col('daily_kw')/1000, 3)
Cast date → StringType, then use substring(col,1,4) for year and substring(col,6,2) for month — works without DateType
Use selectExpr('YEAR(date), MONTH(date), QUARTER(date)') — selectExpr drops every other column, which is fine because the pipeline only needs the temporal fields
fields.correctAnswer: Cast date → DateType, then chain withColumn for year(col), month(col), quarter(col), and round(col('daily_kw')/1000, 3)
fields.rationale: year/month/quarter only work on a DateType column. String slicing is brittle and selectExpr without '*' would lose every other field.

description.context: Four PySpark transformation rules drive most Junior bugs. (1) withColumn's second argument MUST be a Column expression — passing a bare Python string raises an error; use lit('value') to wrap constants. (2) cast() is SILENT on failure — unparseable values become NULL rather than raising NumberFormatException; this is intentional but means bad data hides as nulls. (3) Boolean & with three-valued logic — FALSE & NULL evaluates to FALSE (not NULL), because no matter what NULL would be, FALSE wins; this makes guard expressions like isNotNull() & (col > 0) safe on null rows. (4) withColumn REPLACES an existing column when called with the same name; it does not duplicate. The new DataFrame has the column overwritten in place semantically (the underlying DataFrame is still immutable).
description.task: Predict the behavior of each snippet.
description.validationHint: Pay attention to what lit() does, what happens when cast fails, and how boolean columns interact with null values.

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content: Four code snippets to evaluate; predict the outcome of each.

fields.label: Code: df.withColumn('source', 'bronze_meters') — what happens?
options: A column named 'source' is added with the value 'bronze_meters' in every row; PySpark auto-wraps Python strings as constants.
A TypeError or AssertionError is raised because withColumn's second argument must be a Column expression; the fix is lit('bronze_meters').
The column 'source' is created with null values because Spark cannot interpret the bare string and falls back to null.
The string 'bronze_meters' is interpreted as a column name and Spark errors at analysis time saying that column does not exist.
fields.correctAnswer: A TypeError or AssertionError is raised because withColumn's second argument must be a Column expression; the fix is lit('bronze_meters').
fields.rationale: withColumn requires a Column object as its second argument; bare Python literals are not auto-wrapped. lit() creates a constant Column. The most common Junior confusion is assuming Spark 'just figures out' that you mean a constant; in reality lit() is mandatory because Spark needs a Column expression to add to the plan.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: No auto-wrapping; you must use lit() explicitly.

Option C: The error is at type-check time, not silent null insertion.

Option D: The string is not parsed as a column name; the error is about argument type.

fields.label: A daily_kw column contains the string 'N/A'. After df.withColumn('daily_kw', col('daily_kw').cast('double')), what value does that row's daily_kw contain?
options: The string 'N/A' is preserved because the cast silently fails and keeps the original value untouched.
0.0 because Spark coerces non-numeric strings to zero, treating them as 'no value'.
null because Spark produces NULL whenever a cast cannot parse the source value; the failure is silent.
An exception (NumberFormatException) because the input cannot be cast to a Double.
fields.correctAnswer: null because Spark produces NULL whenever a cast cannot parse the source value; the failure is silent.
fields.rationale: Spark's cast() is INTENTIONALLY forgiving — it returns NULL on parse failure rather than raising. This keeps pipelines from crashing on a single bad row, but it MEANS bad rows hide as nulls. The most common Junior confusion is assuming a noisy failure (exception); in reality the bad data quietly merges with legitimate nulls, and you must compare null counts before/after the cast to detect silent failures.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: cast replaces the column; the original string is gone.

Option B: No coercion to 0; null is the chosen failure value.

Option D: Spark deliberately suppresses cast exceptions to avoid pipeline crashes.

fields.label: An is_valid boolean column is defined as: col('daily_kw').isNotNull() & (col('daily_kw') > 0). For a row where daily_kw is null, what is the value of is_valid?
options: FALSE because isNotNull() returns FALSE on null rows; FALSE & anything is FALSE in three-valued logic, so the second comparison is short-circuited.
NULL because daily_kw > 0 on null evaluates to NULL, and FALSE & NULL propagates as NULL.
TRUE because isNotNull() returning false 'cancels' the null and the chain reverts to the truthy branch.
Raises an exception because col > 0 cannot be evaluated when the value is null.
fields.correctAnswer: FALSE because isNotNull() returns FALSE on null rows; FALSE & anything is FALSE in three-valued logic, so the second comparison is short-circuited.
fields.rationale: Three-valued logic optimizes correctly: FALSE & X is FALSE for any X (including NULL) because the result cannot become TRUE regardless of X. This is actually a HELPFUL property — it lets you write isNotNull() as a guard without worrying about NULL leaking through. The most common Junior confusion is fearing that NULL infects every expression; in fact NULL only leaks where it could matter.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: SQL specifies FALSE & NULL = FALSE specifically to make guards work.

Option C: No 'cancellation' logic; the answer is FALSE, not TRUE.

Option D: Spark handles null comparisons by producing NULL, not by erroring.

fields.label: withColumn('daily_kw', spark_round(col('daily_kw'), 2)) is called on a DataFrame where daily_kw already exists. What happens?
options: Two daily_kw columns appear in the result; Spark allows duplicate column names which causes ambiguity errors later.
An AnalysisException is raised because withColumn() refuses to overwrite an existing column; you must use drop+add explicitly.
The existing daily_kw column is REPLACED with the rounded values in a new DataFrame; column count stays the same.
The original DataFrame is mutated in place with rounded values; the variable still points at the same DataFrame object.
fields.correctAnswer: The existing daily_kw column is REPLACED with the rounded values in a new DataFrame; column count stays the same.
fields.rationale: withColumn(name, expr) adds the column if name is new, REPLACES it if name exists. The result is a new DataFrame (immutability invariant) with the column count unchanged when the name already existed. The most common Junior confusion is assuming withColumn means 'append'; the same method does double duty as add-or-replace, which is why it is the universal column-modification verb.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Spark forbids duplicate column names; withColumn replaces silently.

Option B: withColumn is designed to handle both add and replace cases.

Option D: DataFrames are immutable; the result is a new DataFrame.

tasks.title: Build NordGrid's Complete Meter Enrichment Pipeline

description.context: NordGrid's data engineering team needs a complete enrichment pipeline that transforms raw Bronze meter readings into a fully typed, cleaned, and enriched Silver dataset. The pipeline must handle every data quality issue in the raw CSV: string columns that need casting, inconsistent region formatting, unparseable values that become silent nulls, and the addition of derived fields for downstream consumers.
description.task: Write a pipeline that: (1) reads PS5_data_readings_raw.csv as raw strings (header=True, no inferSchema); (2) casts daily_kw to double; (3) casts date to date type; (4) standardizes region with trim() and upper(); (5) adds a year column from the date; (6) adds a consumption_tier column using when/otherwise: 'low' for < 500, 'medium' for < 2000, 'high' for < 4000, 'critical' otherwise; (7) adds an is_valid boolean flag: true when daily_kw is not null AND daily_kw > 0 AND daily_kw < 10000; (8) adds a pipeline_version column with the constant integer 2 using lit(); (9) selects the final output: meter_id, daily_kw, date, region, year, consumption_tier, is_valid, pipeline_version. Store the result in a variable called silver.
description.validationHint: The output should have 100 rows and 8 columns. The is_valid flag should be false for null, negative, zero, and extreme (>= 10000) readings. Null readings should get consumption_tier = 'critical' (they fall through all when conditions to otherwise).

tasks.partialCredit: 9 independent assertions. Each passed assertion earns 1/9 credit.

conceptsCombined: Type casting with cast() and silent null detection (Lesson 3)
String cleaning with upper() and trim() (Lesson 4)
Boolean flag columns for data quality (Lesson 8)
Final select for output schema contract (Lesson 10)
synthesisNotes.rationale: This task mirrors NordGrid's complete Bronze-to-Silver enrichment pipeline from Lesson 10. The student must combine every major technique from the module into a single pipeline. Key edge cases: (1) null daily_kw values fall through when() to 'critical' tier, (2) is_valid correctly handles nulls because isNotNull is checked first, (3) lit() is required for the constant pipeline_version column. No rows are filtered — this is a pure enrichment pipeline.

fields.label: consumption_tier = 'low' (<500), 'medium' (<2000), 'high' (<4000), 'critical' otherwise. What does NULL daily_kw resolve to?
options: 'critical' — null fails every `<` comparison, so it falls through every when() and lands in otherwise()
null — when() preserves null inputs and returns null on any branch with a null comparison
'low' — Spark treats null as 0, so it matches the first branch (< 500)
fields.correctAnswer: 'critical' — null fails every `<` comparison, so it falls through every when() and lands in otherwise()
fields.rationale: `null < 500` returns null (not true/false); the row never matches a when() and always reaches otherwise(). Spark never coerces null to 0 in numeric comparisons.

selfCheck.foundationModuleException: Not applicable — Module 5 is Core Mechanics phase.
selfCheck.theoryPracticeBoundary: Theory examples use pre-typed Silver data. The practice dataset is raw Bronze strings requiring casting — students must apply cast() themselves rather than starting from pre-typed data. The when/otherwise tier thresholds match the theory (500/2000/4000), but Task 3 tests edge values and null behavior that the theory describes but does not make students calculate. The region cleaning task uses messier data (14 variants vs 4 in the theory) to test transfer of upper()+trim().
selfCheck.datasetNotes: PS5_data_readings_raw.csv has 100 rows with intentionally messy data: all columns are strings, daily_kw has 4 unparseable values that become silent nulls on cast, and region has 14 raw variants that standardize to 4. This forces students to apply every cleaning technique from the module.
